docs.title: 5.4 Operator splitting as a construct (the Stepper and the SplittingCoordinator as syntax)
docs.text:
viva-pde-particle couples its engines with two wrappers whose faces are their children's: Stepper (run a child on every k-th tick of a dt clock, phase-shifted, so that it reads the field at T + (k−1)·dt and has its counts applied at T + k·dt, vcell-fvsolver's lagged coupling) and SplittingCoordinator (run both engines and the adapters in an explicit order over one coupling interval τ = k·dt on a private copy of the stores). The coordinator's schemes are:

Scheme One interval τ = k·dt jacobi PDE for (k−1)·dt; particles for τ reading the field now, update held back; PDE for dt; commit the particles. Equals the two-process composite with the Stepper. gs_particles_first particles for τ; PDE for τ seeing the new particles gs_pde_first PDE for τ; particles for τ seeing the new field strang PDE for τ/2; particles for τ; PDE for τ/2 with the new particles (k even)

Only Jacobi is a per-process clock setting. Gauss–Seidel and Strang are sequential compositions inside one interval: the second engine sees the first one's result before the interval ends, which process-bigraph's scheduler cannot express because every process reads the state at the start of its interval. A splitting scheme is therefore a composition operator over a group of processes, not an attribute of one of them, and the DSL gives it a construct that says the physics as an ordered sequence per coupling interval:

split coupling every 4 * dt {
  run pde for 3 * dt;
  run particles for 4 * dt, hold;   // reads the field now; its update is applied at commit
  run pde for dt;
  commit particles;
}

Gauss–Seidel is run particles for τ; run pde for τ; (or the reverse) and Strang is run pde for τ/2; run particles for τ; run pde for τ/2;. Adapters run whenever a store they read changed, the rule process-bigraph applies to steps, so they need no mention unless an order is pinned. Named schemes are sugar (split coupling every 4 * dt scheme strang { pde, particles }) whose expansion the formatter and hover show. pde and particles are ordinary processes declared in the composite, with static headers.

What the construct buys statically: the participants' config and wires are checked as usual, and the schedule itself is checked, which today happens as ValueErrors in initialize(): each engine's for durations sum to τ per interval, Strang's k is even, every hold has a commit, and the adapters' faces bridge the engines' stores.

What it compiles to: Jacobi can go to the two-process form with the Stepper (the PDE stays a normal process that emitters see every dt); the other schemes go to the SplittingCoordinator node with its pde, particles, adapters and scheme config. The decompiler prints both shapes back as split. Either way the wrappers are desugaring targets and should live in a shared package rather than in viva-pde-particle; if process-bigraph grows ordered sub-steps within an interval, the same text compiles to that instead.

Decisions (2026-10-11): the sequence is optional, the named schemes stay, and no scheme means the lagged Jacobi scheme (split coupling every τ { pde, particles }), which is the coordinator's default and the Stepper form. Scheme names should keep the distinction visible: lagged (viva's jacobi, kept as an alias), sequential with the order, strang.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Superposition on a shared store is native, not split
docs.text:
Several processes adding increments to one store is process-bigraph's default model: the apply semantics for numbers, arrays and maps of them are additive, and every delta that lands at the same time is summed onto the store. Numerically that is simultaneous (Jacobi, additive) splitting, for du/dt = A(u) + B(u) the step u(T+Δ) = u(T) + Δ·A(u(T)) + Δ·B(u(T)), multirate when intervals differ. It needs no construct. What the language says about it is the store's apply semantics, which the type already carries (float and array<float> accumulate, overwrite<T> replaces), and what the checker does about it is the writer analysis of the registry design: two overwriting writers on one store (W221, an ordering race), an additive writer mixed with an overwriting one (W220/E-MIXED-APPLY), and a step publishing a whole array with accumulate semantics (W223). pblang doc lists writers and readers per store with those badges.

split is only for the other coupling style: engines that own their variables and exchange whole values through ports and adapters, where the question is when each engine reads the other's result within an interval.

docs.title: 5.5 Units: declared on stores, polymorphic on components
docs.text:
Units are an annotation on a type, on a store (store conc: map<string, float> @ "uM";) and on a port in a header (fields: map<string, array<float>> @ "uM";). They are data: _units on the bigraph-schema type, checked with pint, never executed. The store is the single source of truth for the composite's unit system; every port wired to it must agree.

Most solvers do not own a unit system. An ODE or PDE engine integrates whatever consistent units the model carries, so its header must not commit to uM. It declares unit variables instead:

process Tellurium at "…" {
  inputs  { species: map<string, float> @ "?U"; time: float @ "?T"; }
  outputs { species: map<string, overwrite<float>> @ "?U"; fluxes: map<string, float> @ "?U/?T"; }
}

?U and ?T are bound per instance from the stores the ports are wired to, the way type variables are inferred: species -> conc binds ?U = uM, time -> clock binds ?T = s, and fluxes -> rates is then checked against uM/s. A variable that only appears in a derived expression is solved for (?T from ?U/?T once ?U is known). This is what "units-of" and "rate-units-of" mean here: @ "?U" is "the units of whatever this is wired to" and @ "?U/?T" is "those units per time unit", with the checker proving the composite consistent without the component naming any unit. If nothing pins a variable the obligation is reported as unresolved, not as an error: a composite with no declared units is unchecked, not wrong.

Findings: W201 unit-mismatch when a bound expression and its store differ, with the conversion factor when the dimensions agree (uM/s into mM/s, factor 0.001: insert an adapter or align the stores) or as incompatible when they do not (uM into kg); I230 when pint cannot parse a unit; I231 when no store pins a variable.

Where an SBML model declares its own unit system, the units belong on the stores the model's species and parameters are mapped to, and they can be generated from the model: the existing SBML stub generator already reads the model file and writes stores with values, and writing their @ units from the model's unit definitions is the same step. A data-level lint that compares a model file's unit definitions with the stores it is wired to is a separate, later check. Pinning a variable explicitly at an instance (units { U = "uM" }) is possible syntax for the case where no store declares units; it is not needed when the stores do.

docs.title: 5.6 Model headers and model sites (SBML and other model files)
docs.text:
The v1 SBML stub generator read a model file and wrote a composite specialized to it: stores named after that model's species and parameters, values baked in. That conflates two things that v2 keeps apart.

A model file has an interface, like a process does. Its species, parameters and compartments with their units, its time unit, and which species are amounts rather than concentrations are the model's face. The model-side twin of describe is describe-model: it reads the file once and writes a model header, a generated, read-only declaration next to the file (Caravagna2010.model.pblang), not a composite:

model Caravagna2010 from "Caravagna2010.xml" {
  time @ "s";
  compartments { compartment: float @ "mL" = 1.0; }
  species { T: float @ "umol/mL" = 1.0; E: float @ "umol/mL" = 1.0; I: float @ "umol/mL" = 1.0; }
  parameters { r2: float = 0.18; b: float = 1.0e-09; … }
  meta { sbml = "L2V4", reactions = 3, events = 0, rules = 0 }
}

Everything in it is data and regenerable; units come from the model's unit definitions, which is where the stores' units in section 5.5 come from. process_bigraph_lang/v2/sbml.py prototypes this on the Caravagna fixture with the standard library's XML parser (no libsbml).

Two kinds of workflow, both first-class.

  • A per-document composite imports the model header and uses it: store species: Caravagna2010.species = Caravagna2010.initial;, a solver wired species -> species, adapters naming real species (substrates { T -> species.T }), emit paths naming real species. The checker verifies all of that statically against the header: a wire to a species the model lacks, a unit mismatch through ?U, an emit path for a species that does not exist.
  • A per-class workflow is a template. The model is a site and the class is the site's sort, what any filler must provide: node model : SBMLModel = ? with a sort that says concentration species in some ?U, a time unit ?T, and the members the workflow touches (parameters.k1 to sweep, species.A for an adapter). The solver's header is polymorphic (?U/?T), the species store is an open map, the model file is a param. Whether a given document fits is a static admits check of its model header against the sort, before anything runs.

Instantiation relates the two: a per-class template plus a model header, with the site filled, is a per-document composite. That is process-bigraph's site-and-fill machinery applied to a data input instead of a process.

What the class can say that v1 could not. The things that decide whether a solver handles a document: amounts versus concentrations (the v1 stub converted by compartment size, silently), events and rules, local parameters, SBML level, version and packages (spatial, comp, fbc). Those become predicates of the model site's sort, and solvers declare what they accept in their headers (accepts: sbml-l3v2, no spatial), so choosing a solver for a model is the same face matching the registry design uses for adapters.

Syntax (implemented in the prototype grammar). A header is model Name from "file" { time @ "…"; compartments {…} species {…} parameters {…} meta {…} }; a sort is the same without from. In a sort, a member named _ stands for every member of its block (species { _: float @ "?U"; ... } says "all species, in one unit ?U"), a block ending in ... admits members the sort does not name, and meta entries are requirements (events = 0, kind = "concentration"). A model site is a store typed by a sort: store model : ODEModel = ?; is open and store model : ODEModel = Caravagna2010; fills it with a header. The checker admits the header against the sort (G301 model-not-admitted for a missing member, an extra member of an exact block or a failed meta requirement; units bind across the whole header, so species in ?U and time in ?T are checked with the same machinery as ports; I232 when the model declares no units for a required member, because an undeclared unit is unknown, not dimensionless). In the document, a filled site becomes the model's blocks as typed stores with the model's values, and an open site becomes a site whose sort is the schema the sort admits.

Units on values that are not stores. Units belong to the type, wherever the value sits: a header's config field can declare dt: float @ "?T" and a param step: float @ "min" referenced as config { dt = ${step} } is then checked against the composite's time unit. Parameter units from a model file are captured when the file declares them and otherwise left undeclared; nothing is ever assumed dimensionless.

Still to do: Name.species-style member types so a composite can type a store by a header's block, and a data-level lint comparing a model file's unit definitions with the stores it is wired to.

docs.title: 6. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Params referenced at several positions in template mode. Substitute at compile time by default (--set); emit same-key multi-sites only if fill_sites confirms multi-fill (a quick test against process_bigraph/templates.py).
  2. Expressions. Allow + - * / on literals and params in every, replicate, shapes and config leaves; the spec projection emits E-SPEC-EXPR unless the expression is a bare param; the template projection evaluates with defaults.
  3. Union syntax. A | B in the DSL (bigraph ~); anonymous struct {a: T; b: U} for merges; raw strings cover the rest.
  4. node vs store for dicts. The edges-inside rule is deterministic; --node-depth N promotes dicts to node for readability without changing meaning.
  5. Untyped stores. W-STORE-UNTYPED with an auto-fix; pblang fmt --infer-types.
  6. Interface resolution. <pkg>/pblang/interfaces.pblang in the wheel plus an entry point; PBLANG_PATH overrides; the catalog aggregates by reading wheels, never by importing.
  7. Units @ "uM". Contract-level metadata (_units in the contract and on array); W-WIRE-UNIT fires only when both ends declare units.
  8. Edge literals in config. Allowed wherever the interface declares an edge or list<edge> field.
  9. shared semantics. Wires on shared_process_ref and where interval lives need confirmation against composite.py.
  10. Doc comments on stores and edges. Text-only until process-bigraph has a convention for state descriptions.
  11. Prototype parser. A small Lark grammar in Python gives text-level round trip quickly; the Langium v2 grammar remains the long-term single source of truth and binds to the same model.

docs.title: v2 implementation plan
docs.text: Status: approved scope for the first round, 2026-10-11. See the research notes, the language design and the registry and authoring design.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
1. This round delivers the design documents (done: this directory) and a round-trip prototype that reads real documents and *.composite.yaml files into a v2 model, prints canonical .pblang v2 text for review, writes an equivalent document back, and proves equivalence. The Langium v2 grammar and the pblang CLI come in later rounds.
  2. The v2 syntax is tree-shaped and mirrors the document.
  3. Interfaces come from generated .pblang interface files (manifest JSON canonical).
  4. The DSL interoperates both ways with CompositeSpec yaml.
  5. The DSL is a verifiable target layer; end users author with registry- and prompt-driven tools.
  6. The language core stays one-to-one with the document. The higher-level semantics it adds are static and compile away: named and imported interfaces, faces as sorts, param, let, edge literals, adapters, units, and referential-integrity checks. There is no pattern or macro layer this round; coupling schemes and engine selection stay in Python builders or composite generators, and the DSL records their result.

Reconciled details:

  • Type spelling in the DSL: int, bool, float, string, map<string, V>, list<T>, maybe<T>, overwrite<T>, enum<a, b>, array<float>[3,3] @ "uM", { a: T; b: U }, A | B, raw "…". The compiler maps int → integer, bool → boolean, map<string, V> → map[V]; unknown names are errors.
  • Error codes: family-prefixed numeric codes with a stable slug (W200 wire-type-mismatch); the mnemonic names in the language design are the slugs.
  • emit: emit parquet { … } with { … }; or emit "local:ParquetEmitter" { … };.
  • Interfaces in decompiled text: resolved addresses print import pkg.{Name}; unresolved ones print an inline declaration from _inputs/_outputs and at "…".
  • Parsing this round: the model is the pivot; text is printed and snapshotted. A Lark parser is a stretch step; the Langium grammar remains the long-term source of truth and binds to the same model.
  • Dependencies: no version bump of process-bigraph or bigraph-schema (nothing needed is 1.7-only). bigraph-schema moves to the main dependencies; process-bigraph stays dev-only (the package returns plain dicts); pyyaml and types-PyYAML join the dev group.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
process_bigraph_lang/v2/ (shipped; mypy strict and ruff apply; it outlives the prototype as the target of the later Langium v2 AST binder):

Module Responsibility model.py dataclasses Document, Composite, Store, Node, Edge, Site, Face, Param, Emitter, Import, InterfaceDecl, Address, ParamRef, ExternalRef, Path; MISSING sentinel; no bigraph imports types.py TypeExpr tree (Named, Struct, Union, Group, Raw); parse_type(str \| dict) via bigraph_schema.parse.parse_expression; to_bigraph(); to_surface() values.py predicates, tuple and ndarray handling, externalization thresholds paths.py Path.from_wire / to_wire; reuses compiler.generator.compute_relative_path reader.py read_document({schema, state}) for authoring and saved forms; read_composite_spec(dict) writer.py write_document(Document, assets=…) → {schema, state, **options}; write_composite_spec(Document) printer.py print_document(Document) → (text, assets) normalize.py normalize_document, equivalent, diff_documents __main__.py python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 compile \| decompile \| check \| diff \| describe …

Reused from v1 without copying: compiler/converter.py (edge_address, site, set_value_at_path, get_value_at_path) and compiler/generator.py (compute_relative_path; type_schema as the reference for string vs dict type emission). v1 stays untouched and green.

docs.title: Reader rules
docs.text:
Walk state and schema in parallel, state key order first. Classify each key in order:

  1. Site: _type == "site" → Store(site=Site(sort, default)).
  2. Edge: _type in process/step, or address present, or the schema entry says edge. Kind from state _type → schema _type → interval present → process → priority/_triggers → step → else ValueError naming the path. address from "proto:data", dict, ${x} or site. Consume config, inputs, outputs, interval, priority, _triggers, _inputs/_outputs (→ ports); drop instance and _contract; everything else → extras verbatim. Short name Composite → inner from config.state/config.schema, bridge, interface. A Stepper-style child {address, config} inside config stays a plain struct value (lossless).
  3. Node: a dict with an edge or site descendant, or a struct schema, or a map schema of edges (Node(type=…)).
  4. Store: everything else; typed from the schema when present; schema-only → value=MISSING.

Saved form is auto-detected (root global_time, dict addresses, _contract): also drop root global_time, take edge _type from the schema entry, ignore the schema's inputs: "wires" entries, parse string _inputs/_outputs, keep fully defaulted config verbatim. Params come only from CompositeSpec parameters; ^\$\{(\w+)\}$ strings become ParamRef, embedded ones ParamRef(template=…), undeclared ones are errors. Imports come from local:!a.b.C addresses (collisions print fully qualified); local:Name prints as Name with no import. Interface declarations are emitted only for edges that carry ports. CompositeSpec metadata (name, description, tags, requires, emitters, global_time_precision) is read; other keys go to extras.

docs.title: Printer rules
docs.text: Order: a header comment naming the source; sorted imports; params; interface declarations in first-use order; composite name "description" { requires {…} options {…} stores and sites, then nodes, then edges, each in source order }; emit …. Two-space indent; a block prints inline when it fits in 100 columns and no nested block broke. Values: ints as ints, floats via repr, true/false/null, JSON-escaped double-quoted strings, lists […], tuples (…) (preserved so v1 parity holds), struct literals when all keys are identifiers else map literals, ${dt}, ? and ?(default). Arrays and nested lists with more than 100 elements and strings longer than 1000 characters are externalized to <snapshot>.assets/<path-slug>.json|txt (JSON {dtype, shape, data} for diffability; ExternalRef keeps a $bundle_ref-compatible key) and printed as array(file("…"), dtype = "float64", shape = [11, 11, 3]) or file("…"); small arrays print inline with an array(…) wrapper. Port overrides print as ports { … }; unknown keys print as extra { … } or schema { … } as explicit "not understood" markers. A saved nested composite with empty inner state prints a // WARNING: inner state lost by Composite.save comment.

docs.title: Writer rules
docs.text:
Schema half: Store.type → to_bigraph with the default folded as {"_type": T, "_default": d} (v1's exact shape); untyped stores → no entry; sites → no schema entry (process-bigraph#213); Node → nested dict or {"_type":"map","_value":…}; edges → no schema entry; schema_extras merged back. State half: values; sites via converter.site; edges {"_type", "_inputs"/"_outputs", "address", "config" (omit empty), "inputs"/"outputs" (omit empty), "interval"/"priority"/"_triggers", **extras}; a nested composite → config = {state, schema?, bridge, interface, …}. ParamRef → "${name}"; ExternalRef → loaded through the assets callback. write_composite_spec → {name, description, tags, requires, parameters {type (normalized bycomposite_spec.normalize_type), default, description, choices}, emitters [{address, paths ["a/b"], config?}], schema?, state, global_time_precision?, **extras}; tests dump it with yaml.safe_dump(sort_keys=False) and feed CompositeSpec.from_dict(...).to_document(emit=False).

Parity target: write_document(read_document(doc)) == doc exactly for every v1 expected template in tests/compiler/generator/ (toy add-floats, test_collections flat/list/map, spatio-flux I/II/III, test_open_values_compile_to_template_sites).

docs.title: Normalizer (behaviour verified against the installed versions)
docs.text:
normalize_document(doc, core): in the schema half drop global_time, move edge entries to a side table ({path: {_type, _inputs, _outputs}}), and render other entries with core.render(core.access(entry), defaults=True), falling back to a canonical sorted dict when access raises on an unknown dict-form type (string names pass through); a rendered string containing a top-level | or : is re-accessed to dict form so "x:float|y:float" and {"x":"float","y":"float"} collide. In the state half drop root global_time; render sites with _sort canonicalized; edges become {_type (state or side table), address as "proto:data", _inputs/_outputs canonical (omitted if absent on both), config canonical (omit {}), inputs/outputs canonical wires (str → [str]; omit empty), interval/priority as float, _triggers}; drop instance and _contract; recurse into nested local:Composite config. Values: tuple → list, ndarray → tolist(), numpy scalars → Python, floats compared with math.isclose(rel_tol=1e-9). diff_documents flattens to state/smoldyn/config/dt-style paths and prints -, +, ~ lines (capped at 200), falling back to a unified JSON diff.

Ignored: key order, tuple vs list, dtype, runtime keys, string vs structured forms of addresses, wires and types, absent vs {} config, default-in-schema vs float{…}, schema edge entries. Not ignored: config values. A stronger realized_equivalent(a, b, core) (tests only) builds Composite from both and compares serialize_state() and serialize_schema() through the same normalizer.

docs.title: Status (2026-10-11)
docs.text:
Steps 0–9 are implemented on the v2-design branch: the package, the tests, the corpus (all six entries, the hybrid fixture generated in the viva-pde-particle environment), the snapshots and the print/diff entry point. The snapshots in tests/fixtures/data/v2/snapshots/ are the material for the design review. Observations from printing the corpus that feed back into the design:

  • The hybrid repeats the same grid literal in four places; the let hoisting in the design (section 2.3) is worth doing early, and the Stepper child prints as a plain { address, config } struct until edge literals exist.
  • Multi-line strings (the generated Smoldyn config) must be externalized at a much lower threshold than other text.
  • Reading from a CompositeSpec alone leaves stores untyped (store molecule_counts = {};), which is exactly the W-STORE-UNTYPED case; types will come from interface files (stretch step 10).
  • The saved form of a nested composite reads back with an empty inner composite; the printer flags it.

Stretch step 10 is also done in a minimal form: process_bigraph_lang/v2/interfaces.py has describe_module (stage A over a Python module: portable address, config_schema, ports obtained with the class standing in for self, dynamic_ports when that fails, the docstring), an InterfaceRegistry with a JSON manifest (pblang-manifest/0), and python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 describe <module> --manifest m.json --out m.pblang. The printer resolves edge addresses against a registry and prints import module.{Name}; instead of an inline declaration; the spatio-flux and saved-toy snapshots show it, and toy_library.interfaces.pblang is the first generated interface file.

Stretch step 11 is done too: process_bigraph_lang/v2/parser.py is a Lark LALR grammar for the printed subset (imports, params, meta/options, inline interface declarations, stores, nodes, edges, nested composites with bridges, sites, ports, extra, schema, emit, the array(...)/file(...) value forms, and the type spelling). Every committed snapshot parses back into a model that prints to the same text and writes a document equivalent to the corpus original (tests/v2/test_parser.py), so the round trip now runs from text. The grammar is the executable form of the sketch in the design and the acceptance spec for the Langium v2 grammar. Not covered yet: expressions, replicate, {default} suffixes on types, when / of config.x faces, and hand-written override files for dynamic ports.

Headers for a real package exist too: tests/fixtures/data/v2/interfaces/ holds the interface files and manifest that python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 describe generated from viva-pde-particle's classes inside its own environment (the publish-time step). Against them, the hybrid prints with imports, and process_bigraph_lang/v2/check.py (python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 check doc.json --interfaces m.json) verifies a document statically, with no process code imported: unknown ports (S021), missing or unknown config keys (T121, S022), wires that name no declared store (W211), wire type mismatches against declared store types (W200), paths escaping the root (E110), an interval on a step (T130), unknown components (S020), dynamic ports (I210) and untyped stores (I220). On the hybrid it finds the particle_positions store that nothing declares and the three components whose ports only an instance can tell.

The checker also does the writer analysis of the registry design: per store, who writes it and with which apply semantics (from the port type, or the store's own overwrite<T>); W220 (info) lists additive writers whose contributions superpose, W221 warns when an overwriting writer sits next to any other writer (order-dependent), and W223 warns when a step publishes an array-typed value with accumulate semantics. emit declarations are checked too: W240 when a path names no declared store (the emitter would record an empty value) and W241 (info) when an emitted store is written by nothing. Units are checked with pint: port units may contain unit variables (?U, ?U/?T) bound per instance from the wired stores, so a solver that works in any consistent unit system is still checked; W201 reports a mismatch with the conversion factor or as incompatible.

Making the headers static was a change to the wrapped package, not to the tooling: on viva-pde-particle's static-interfaces branch, SmoldynHybrid always declares particle_positions (the emit_positions flag only decides whether the value is produced) and SpatialRecorder became GridRecorder and MeshRecorder with one fixed face each. The regenerated headers have no ... except on Stepper and SplittingCoordinator, the scheduling wrappers whose face is their child's. process_bigraph_lang/v2/graph.py then produces a viewer's wiring graph (nodes with typed ports, stores, edges, nested children) from a document and the headers alone, which is what a loom-style viewer needs to run without a Python environment that has the processes installed.

Two decisions made while building the parser: the normalizer canonicalizes types from the parsed type tree rather than through bigraph-schema's renderer (the renderer drops custom type names such as positive_float and fails on unknown dict-form types, so the two spellings of one type no longer collided), and /// doc comments are joined with spaces when parsed because the printer wraps them.

describe-model (process_bigraph_lang/v2/sbml.py, python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 describe-model x.xml) is the model-side twin of describe: it reads an SBML file with the standard library and writes a model header (time unit, compartments, species as concentrations or amounts, parameters, each with pint-readable units composed from the model's unit definitions, plus reaction/event/rule counts and the SBML level, version and packages). The Caravagna header is snapshotted; see the design's section 5.6 for how per-document composites and per-class templates use it.

The grammar has model declarations (headers and sorts), store m : Sort = Header | ?; model sites, and the checker admits a header against a sort (G301, units bound across the header) and checks config values that reference a param against the header's config units; the writer expands a filled model site into the model's typed blocks. The Caravagna header parses back and prints the same declaration.

The Langium v2 grammar exists (dsl/src/language/pblang-v2.langium, language id pblang-v2, files .pbl), coexisting with v1 in the same language server, VS Code extension and CLI. It parses every snapshot with no parse or linking errors (dsl/test/v2/), and process_bigraph_lang/v2/langium.py binds its JSON AST to the same model the Lark grammar builds; tests/v2/test_langium.py requires identical prints from both. Not yet in the Langium side at that point: validators beyond parsing and name resolution, hover and completion, and the cutover of .pblang to v2.

The checker was then ported to TypeScript (dsl/src/language/v2/{types,headers,units,check,validator}.ts) and registered as a Langium validation of V2Module, so the editor, the browser and the CLI (check --json) share one implementation; the Lark parser and the Python checker were retired, and process_bigraph_lang/v2/langium.py and check.py call cli-native. The compliance suite moved to dsl/test/v2/check.test.ts case for case; the Python tests keep the same expectations through the CLI. lark and pint are no longer dependencies. One semantic change surfaced by the shipped growth-division example: a wire to .. from a root edge is the idiom for "the parent store", which process-bigraph resolves by clamping at the root, so going above the root is W110, a warning, rather than an error.

Hover and completion followed (dsl/src/language/v2/{resolve,hover,completion}.ts, see the design's section 5.3, "Editor services"), and header files open in the workspace now answer imports in the editor (V2Registry falls back to the index of V2Interface declarations by module).

Decided 2026-10-12: the Python datamodel is not a public target. First process_bigraph_lang.v2 exposed compile_text / compile_file (text -> parse -> check -> document or CompositeSpec, CompileError on errors) and decompile (document or CompositeSpec -> text) over an internal model; then the model moved: reader, writer, printer and binder are TypeScript (dsl/src/language/v2/{model,json,paths,reader,writer, printer,bind,graph,modelheader,yaml}.ts) behind cli-native compile | decompile | headers | model-header | graph, and the Python package keeps only the wrappers (api.py), describe (introspection), describe-model (SBML as JSON) and the normalizer. model.py, reader.py, writer.py, printer.py, paths.py, values.py and graph.py are gone; types.py stays as the normalizer's and describe's type parser. The snapshot and round-trip tests under tests/v2/ run through the CLI; dsl/test/v2/{roundtrip,model}.test.ts check the same snapshots byte for byte on the TypeScript side (every corpus document prints to its snapshot; every snapshot is a fixpoint; the v1 expected documents write back exactly). The cutover followed: .pblang is the v2 language (.pbl is still accepted), and v1 is gone, the grammar, its validators, the SBML stub command, the Python compiler and parser bridge, the ANTLR grammar and its generated parsers, and their tests. The v1 expected documents live on as tests/fixtures/data/v2/corpus/v1/. The language id pblang-v2 and the V2 rule prefix were then renamed: the language id is pblang, the grammar is pblang.langium (grammar Pblang), its rules are Module, Store, ... and consumers import the generated AST as a namespace (ast.Store) because its names coincide with the object model's.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Render quirks (handled by re-render and re-access; covered by tests); local:Name vs local:!path (kept verbatim; the printer only imports ! forms; the writer never rewrites); nested-composite save loss (authoring documents only; negative test); numpy in config and state (tolist plus isclose; array(…) wrapper or sidecar); saved-form config bloat (equality only claimed after normalization); deptry and mypy (no process_bigraph import in the package; yaml test-only); snapshot churn (fixed ordering and repr floats; explicit regeneration flag); prettier reformatting the copied yaml (accepted; noted in the corpus README).

These are sequenced in the roadmap of the registry and authoring design.

docs.title: v2 registry, prompt-guided authoring and validation UX
docs.text:
Status: design, 2026-10-11. Companion to the language design; background in the research notes; sequencing in the plan.

The framing: the formal DSL is a verifiable target, not the single document an end user constructs by hand. End-user authoring uses (1) a declared registry of components (processes, steps, adapters, emitters) whose interfaces are published as data, so authoring needs no Python import or introspection, and (2) prompts (LLM-guided tooling such as the viva-superpowers Claude Code skills) that guide construction, documentation and validation. The DSL is where the constructed workflow is type-checked, contract-audited, explained and documented, and from which the runnable document or *.composite.yaml is generated.

docs.title: 0. Shape
docs.text:
package repo CI (package's own env)        anywhere pblang is installed              execution env
pblang-describe (stage A: introspect)  ->  pblang registry build (stage B)          pblang preflight
   manifest.raw.json                        + interfaces.override.pblang              (installed vs lock vs
                                            -> pblang/manifest.json                    fingerprint; env hints)
                                            -> pblang/interfaces.pblang
viva-catalog nightly: fetch manifest.json per module -> components.json
LLM skill or human: import -> draft .pblang -> pblang check / doc / compile -> preflight -> run

Three principles:

  1. The manifest JSON is canonical; interfaces.pblang is rendered from it deterministically. Tools read JSON, humans and import read .pblang, CI verifies they agree.
  2. Stage A has zero pblang dependencies, so it runs inside any package environment (a pixi env, the workbench env_worker, a git: per-SHA venv).
  3. One diagnostics JSON format for the CLI, the language server, the workbench and the skills.

docs.title: 1.1 Files shipped by a package
docs.text:
<pkg>/pblang/manifest.json               generated, canonical (stage B output); committed and in the wheel
<pkg>/pblang/interfaces.pblang           rendered from manifest.json; what `import` reads
<pkg>/pblang/interfaces.override.pblang  hand-written; merged by component name; committed
<pkg>/pblang/manifest.raw.json           stage A output; CI artifact only

They are located without importing the package, through importlib.metadata.distribution(name).files. That is the difference from bigraph_schema/package/discover.py and the workbench's env_worker.py, which both import.

docs.title: 1.2 Manifest (design target; what ships is section 1.7)
docs.text:
The fields below are the target for later versions of the shared format that section 1.7 describes (shipping: pbg-interfaces/1, with its JSON Schema in docs/schemas/).

{
  "schema_version": "pbg-interfaces/2",
  "package": {
    "name": "viva-pde-particle",
    "module": "viva_pde_particle",
    "version": "0.4.2",
    "python": ">=3.11",
    "source": "https://github.com/vivarium-collective/viva-pde-particle",
    "ref": "v0.4.2",
    "commit": "e5325c1"
  },
  "generated": {
    "tool": "pblang-describe 0.1.0",
    "at": "2026-10-11T00:00:00Z",
    "process_bigraph": "1.8.5",
    "bigraph_schema": "1.7.0",
    "from_override": ["Stepper", "SplittingCoordinator"]
  },
  "environment": {
    "install": ["pip install viva-pde-particle==0.4.2"],
    "native": ["smoldyn (patched fork)", "dolfinx", "gmsh"],
    "image": "ghcr.io/vivarium-collective/viva-pde-particle:0.4.2",
    "platforms": ["linux-x86_64", "macos-arm64"],
    "rest": { "port": 8000, "entry": "viva_pde_particle.server:app" },
    "git_entry": "viva_pde_particle.pblang_entry:make_process"
  },
  "types": [
    { "name": "positive_float", "schema": { "_type": "float" }, "opaque": true }
  ],
  "components": []
}

A component entry is a superset of the workbench's RegistryProcess so the workbench can adopt it unchanged:

{
  "name": "GridCountsToMeshConcentration",
  "address": "local:!viva_pde_particle.steps.transfer.GridCountsToMeshConcentration",
  "aliases": ["GridCountsToMeshConcentration"],
  "kind": "adapter",
  "base": "step",
  "config_schema": { "grid": "map", "mesh": "map", "species": "list[string]" },
  "config_docs": {
    "grid": "CartesianGrid spec (origin, size, shape)",
    "mesh": "mesh spec"
  },
  "ports": {
    "inputs": { "particle_counts": "map[array[float]]" },
    "outputs": { "particle_conc": "map[overwrite[array[float]]]" }
  },
  "port_semantics": {
    "outputs": { "particle_conc": "overwrite" },
    "inputs": { "particle_counts": "read" }
  },
  "dynamic_ports": { "dynamic": false },
  "contract": {},
  "interval": { "configurable": false },
  "docs": {
    "summary": "Grid particle counts to P1 mesh concentration (P^T).",
    "source": "steps/transfer.py:140"
  },
  "examples": [
    "viva_pde_particle/composites/hybrid.py#build_mesh_hybrid_document"
  ],
  "adapter": {},
  "fingerprint": "sha256:…"
}

kind is one of process | step | adapter | emitter | visualization | draft | composite_generator | composite | type. composite_generator entries carry parameters, emitters, builder and tags; composite entries copy the package's *.composite.yaml fields. fingerprint is the sha256 of the canonical JSON of {address, config_schema, ports} and is what preflight compares.

dynamic_ports has three shapes: {"dynamic": false}; {"dynamic": true, "depends_on": ["emit_positions"], "how": "defaults", "note": "…"} (ports listed are those obtained with default config; the checker hints when those keys are set); {"dynamic": true, "rule": "union_of_children", "children_key": "process"} (Stepper) or "adapters" plus "pde", "particles" (SplittingCoordinator): ports are computed from the DSL edge literals once the children's manifests are imported.

A first generated example lives in the repository: tests/fixtures/data/v2/interfaces/ holds the interface files and viva_pde_particle.manifest.json that python -m process_bigraph_lang.v2 describe produced from viva-pde-particle's classes in that package's own environment. They show the honest output for ports the generator cannot see (inputs { ... } plus a // TODO: dynamic ports note on Stepper, SmoldynHybrid and SpatialRecorder), and process_bigraph_lang/v2/check.py uses them to verify the hybrid composite without importing process code.

docs.title: 1.3 Stage A: pblang-describe
docs.text:
A tiny distribution (packages/pblang-describe/; deps: process-bigraph and bigraph-schema only). CLI: python -m pblang_describe --package viva_pde_particle [--core viva_pde_particle.core:build_core] [--build-generators] -o manifest.raw.json. Per package:

  1. Enumerate Edge subclasses of the package's own modules (the find_edges logic from bigraph_schema/package/discover.py, filtered by module prefix), never allocate_core() over all distributions. Use the package's build_core() if given, else a plain core plus its register_types hook.
  2. Copy config_schema as authored and also run core.access on it, recording config_schema_errors[] (this is where int and any are caught at publish time).
  3. Ports by a ladder, recording which rung succeeded in dynamic_ports.how: DraftProcess attributes → cls.inputs(cls) with the class as self → instantiate with core.default(config_schema) and call inputs()/outputs() → override file → null with the exception text. Rungs that disagree mark dynamic: true; depends_on comes from an AST scan of inputs/outputs for self.config[...] keys (the technique process_bigraph/contract_drift.py already uses).
  4. port_semantics: overwrite if the type contains overwrite[, set if the resolved schema replaces, else accumulate; read for inputs. An optional class attribute port_semantics = {...} overrides.
  5. contract: resolve_contract(...) serialized, with the audit_contract/completeness grade.
  6. kind: emitter (plus EmitterContract fields when viva-emitters is present), visualization, adapter (class attribute adapter), draft, else by MRO.
  7. Composite generators and *.composite.yaml, restricted to the package.
  8. Never abort on one class: per-component errors[], overall status: ok|partial.

docs.title: 1.4 Stage B: pblang registry build and verify
docs.text: pblang registry build <pkg-dir> reads manifest.raw.json, parses interfaces.override.pblang with the normal grammar, merges by name (override wins per field: ports, docs, adapter, dynamic_ports, contract rows), fills git ref and commit, computes fingerprints, writes manifest.json and renders interfaces.pblang with a header naming the manifest hash. pblang registry verify rebuilds in a temporary directory and diffs; it is the CI gate.

docs.title: 1.5 CI and the catalog
docs.text:
• Per repo: a reusable publish-interfaces.yml published from viva-catalog and scaffolded by pbg-template. On push to main and on tag: install the package in its own env, run stage A, pipx run process-bigraph-lang registry build, verify; bot-commit pblang/* on main if stale; attach the manifest and interface file as release assets. The wheel includes pblang/* as package data.
  • viva-catalog nightly: for each modules.json entry fetch <source>/<ref>/<package>/pblang/manifest.json; aggregate into ecosystem-interfaces.json and a flat components.json for search. Packages without a manifest keep their AST-scanned entry marked "interface": "unpublished". This replaces the closed PR's idea of AST-extracted ports.

docs.title: 1.6 Versioning and staleness
docs.text:
• import pkg; with an optional @range. Resolution order: explicit paths from pblang.toml → the installed distribution's manifest (via importlib.metadata, no import) → the catalog cache (pblang registry fetch).
  • Lock file <workflow>.pblang.lock.json (pblang-lock/1): package version, ref, commit, manifest sha, and component fingerprints. pblang lock writes it; pblang check warns on drift.
  • pblang preflight in the execution env compares the installed version to the lock, then runs stage A for only the referenced classes and compares fingerprints, reporting a port-level diff when an interface is stale.

docs.title: 1.7 What ships today: the shared interface manifest (pbg-interfaces/1), one per environment
docs.text:
Decided 2026-10-12 (see the stage two plan). Sections 1.1 to 1.6 remain the target; what exists is smaller, and two decisions shape it.

A manifest describes an environment, not a package. describe must import the classes inside the environment that will run the document, and environments differ (compose-api's shared image carries process-bigraph 1.0.5, viva-pde-particle's image 1.8.x and its own core).

The format is shared, not this DSL's. It is named for the process-bigraph ecosystem (pbg-interfaces), carries no .pblang syntax, and has a published JSON Schema: pbg-interfaces-1.schema.json (https://biosimulations.github.io/process-bigraph-lang/schemas/pbg-interfaces-1.schema.json, which each manifest names in $schema). Types stay in bigraph-schema's own string or dict forms and addresses in process-bigraph's local:!module.Class form, exactly as the classes declare them, and the component keys follow the workbench's registry (name, address, kind, description, config_schema, inputs, outputs). So any tool that reads a bigraph-schema type can use a manifest as it is: a core's access, the workbench, compose-api, a prompt-driven skill, another checker. Readers ignore keys they do not know, so a producer may add more.

  • Producer. process_bigraph_lang/v2/describe_env.py is stage A in its smallest form: one file, standard library only, importing nothing from this package, so it runs as a plain script in any image or env: python describe_env.py viva_pde_particle --env-name viva-pde-particle --image <ref> > manifest.json. It imports every module under the given roots (a failed import is recorded, never fatal), keeps the step and process classes each module defines, and shares its per-class code with describe_module. compose-api runs it in CI inside each environment it offers and serves the result at GET /registry/environments/{name}/manifest.
  • Consumers here. Pblang.addManifest / setManifests (main thread) and the language server's pblang/setManifests notification (SET_MANIFESTS_NOTIFICATION; a host editor sends it when the environment is known or changes, and every open document is re-checked); the CLI's --interfaces. A component with a known address replaces the earlier one. The earlier, pblang-only pblang-manifest/0 (config: {key: {type, default}}, doc) is still read; anything else is rejected.
Key Content $schema, schema_version the schema's URL; "pbg-interfaces/1" environment {name, image, python, process_bigraph, bigraph_schema, packages {dist: version}, roots, generated_by} (from describe_env.py) components[] one per step or process class, sorted by address .name, .kind, .address, .module class name; process or step (by MRO); local:!module.Class; the defining module .description the first paragraph of the class docstring, when there is one .config_schema the class's config_schema as authored, key by key (null for a value that is not a type expression); a default is in the type .inputs, .outputs {port: type} from inputs() / outputs() called with the class as self; null when they need an instance .dynamic_ports true when the ports need an instance (config-dependent or children's) errors[] {module, error} per module or class that failed (from describe_env.py)

Not yet in version 1, compared with section 1.2: units and contracts, port semantics, adapter metadata, fingerprints. Section 1.2 is the design target for later versions of this same format.

docs.title: 2. Adapters as first-class entries
docs.text:
An adapter is a step whose purpose is to map one face to another (grid particle counts → mesh concentration field). Metadata, declared as a class attribute adapter = {…} or in the override file:

{
  "from": {
    "port": "particle_counts",
    "layout": "grid",
    "quantity": "count",
    "units": "molecule"
  },
  "to": {
    "port": "particle_conc",
    "layout": "mesh_p1",
    "quantity": "concentration",
    "units": "uM"
  },
  "shared_config": ["grid", "mesh", "species"],
  "method": "transpose interpolation P^T",
  "exact": false,
  "conserves": ["mass"],
  "cost": "O(n_grid)"
}

Non-adapter ports carry _layout and _quantity rows in the contract's documentary port dicts (free-form per ProcessContract, ignored by existing code). A controlled vocabulary lives in docs/vocab/faces.json (layouts scalar, grid, mesh_p1, mesh_dg0, positions, per_species_map; quantities count, concentration, amount, rate, flux, field, positions, time; x- extensions). viva-pde-particle's DESIGN.md §13 component contract maps directly onto it.

pblang suggest-adapter scores adapters by layout and quantity match (required), unit convertibility (pint), and core.resolve on both sides, and returns ranked candidates with the shared config to fill and an insertable DSL snippet. A check (W230) fires when an adapter's shared config literal differs from the producer's.

docs.title: 3.1 Tool surface
docs.text:
Every command takes --json; exit 0 clean, 1 diagnostics with errors, 2 usage or internal error.

Command Output pblang registry search <q> [--kind] [--tag] [--input-type] [--output-type] [--face face.json] ranked components; face mode is find_candidates semantics over manifests, no import pblang registry show <ref> full entry, rendered declaration, a minimal instantiation snippet, dynamic_ports explanation pblang registry fetch / build / verify / sources lock-style records, verify diff pblang check <file> [--level parse\|scope\|types\|wiring\|ground\|env] diagnostics document (§4.5) pblang explain <CODE> {code, title, why, fix, example_before, example_after, links}; the same text the LSP shows on hover pblang suggest-adapter <file> --from a.port --to b.port candidates with why, shared_config, snippet and LSP edits pblang fmt <file> canonical text pblang compile <file> --to yaml\|document\|template [--params k=v] [--exec-plan local\|rest\|git] -o out the artifact plus a source map out.pblang.map.json (document path → DSL range) pblang decompile <x.composite.yaml\|doc.json> -o file.pblang best-effort text plus a list of what could not be expressed pblang doc <file> --format md\|json\|html Markdown narrative plus graph JSON (§3.3) pblang preflight <file> [--python <exe>] [--suggest-env] §5 pblang lock <file> lock file

docs.title: 3.2 Skill flow (/viva-compose, in viva-superpowers)
docs.text:
1. Orient: `pblang registry sources`, `pblang registry search --json <intent keywords>`; with --from, `pblang decompile`.
2. Select: for each role (engine, adapter, emitter) `registry show`; prefer kind=adapter for face gaps; never invent ports.
3. Draft: write <slug>.pblang (file-level `///` intent, `param` for anything a study would vary, `emit` for observables).
4. Fix loop (bounded): `pblang check --json`; apply `fix.edits` when present, else `pblang explain CODE`;
   wiring warnings -> `pblang suggest-adapter`; groundness -> ask the user or `?(default)`; stop at zero errors.
5. Document: `pblang doc -o <slug>.md`; present the DSL and the doc to the user; wait for approval.
6. Materialize: `pblang lock`; `pblang compile --to yaml -o composites/<slug>.composite.yaml`.
7. Preflight: `pblang preflight --json`; report missing packages with the manifest's install hints; hand off to the run skill.
Hard gates: never hand-edit the generated .composite.yaml; never silence a diagnostic by widening a type.

Sibling skills: /viva-publish-interfaces (runs stage A and B in a package repo and opens the override file for anything with ports: null or dynamic: true) and /viva-adapt (a thin wrapper on suggest-adapter).

docs.title: 3.3 Documentation generation
docs.text: pblang doc merges three sources: /// doc comments, registry docs and contracts per component, and the wiring graph from the compiled model. Markdown sections: Overview; Parameters (name, type, default, units, doc); Components (name, kind, package@version, interval, summary); Stores (type, units, writers → readers with overwrite/accumulate badges); Wiring narrative per store; Open sites; Diagnostics summary; Provenance (lock entries, pblang version, manifest hashes). Graph JSON {nodes, stores, edges, groups} feeds a small adaptor for loom and bigraph_viz. The user reviews the .pblang and the Markdown; the .composite.yaml is a build artifact with a header naming its source and a CI check that regenerates and diffs it.

docs.title: 4.1 Layers and code families
docs.text:
Codes carry a family prefix and a stable slug (W200 wire-type-mismatch).

Layer Where Family Examples (message → fix hint) Parse Langium and CLI P0xx P001 expected '}' Scope and imports Langium and Python resolver S0xx S010 package 'viva_smoldyn' not found in any registry source → fetch hint; S011 lock pins 0.3.1, resolved 0.4.0; S020 unknown component → did-you-mean; S021 unknown port, noting dynamic_ports.depends_on; S022 unknown config key Types Python core seeded with manifest types T1xx T100 unknown type 'int' → "bigraph-schema has 'integer'"; T110 value 3 is not a float; T120 config 'species' expects list[string]; T140 opaque type checked loosely (info) Wiring and contract Python W2xx W200 wire type mismatch via core.resolve_schemas; W201 unit mismatch; W210 port bound twice; W211 required input unbound; W220 two accumulating writers on store; W221 overwrite writer plus another writer; W223 step publishes a whole array with accumulate semantics → "did you mean overwrite[...]"; W230 adapter shared config differs; W240 emit path matches no store; W241 observable never written Groundness Python (open_sites, admits_why, registry_dependent_addresses) G3xx G300 required site unfilled; G301 filler rejected (text from admits_why); G302 non-portable address → local:!… from the manifest Env preflight Python, execution env E4xx E400 not installed + install lines; E401 version differs from lock; E402 interface stale with a port diff; E403 address unresolvable in core; E404 native dependency import failed Runtime wrapper around Composite R5xx process-bigraph exceptions mapped through the source map to a DSL range

docs.title: 4.2 Additive vs overwrite
docs.text: The registry records port_semantics per port; rendered interfaces show it. The checker builds the store graph statically (like process_bigraph/composite_audit.py) and emits W220, W221 and W223; pblang explain W223 carries the one-paragraph explanation of bigraph-schema's apply semantics with before and after snippets.

docs.title: 4.3 Reuse of bigraph-schema and process-bigraph
docs.text: Type names through core.access on a validation core (rejecting on exception instead of passing strings through); wire types through core.resolve_schemas; units and ranges through units_compatible and range_subsumes; sites through admits_why and required_open_sites; addresses through registry_dependent_addresses and unresolvable_addresses; contract grades copied into manifests at publish time.

docs.title: 4.4 TypeScript and Python
docs.text: Decided 2026-10-12: the checker is TypeScript, inside the Langium services, because its inputs are data (the document and header manifests) and a browser must validate without a round trip. Python does what needs an environment: describe, saved documents with numpy, equivalence through a core, groundness, preflight, running. A browser-based authoring tool therefore needs a Python-backed API only for those environment-bound operations. The earlier plan (Langium for syntax only, Python for the type algebra, the language server shelling out to pblang check on save) is superseded by that decision. Manifests reach the checker as data: through --interfaces in the CLI, addManifest/setManifests in the API, and pblang/setManifests in a language server (section 1.7).

docs.title: 5. Execution without one giant environment
docs.text:
Interfaces being data removes the package from the authoring loop. For running, the manifest environment field maps to options:

Option Manifest fields Use Local env with everything installed install preflight reports E4xx with install lines; --suggest-env writes a merged requirements or pixi fragment rest: process servers rest.port, image compile --exec-plan rest --endpoint pkg=URL rewrites addresses; one container per package image via compose-api; face conformance at bind git: per-SHA venv git_entry, source, commit needs a make_process(name, config) entry convention; defer Whole-composite image each package's image not realistic; prefer rest:

First step: the environment field plus pblang preflight. Then rest:, which already exists and matches the workbench and compose-api direction.
